title: Ruth Gleans in the Field of Boaz

date.label: Undated Ruth narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Ruth 2 is one complete harvest-season episode: a single detailed day in the field (vv. 4–17) closed by a season summary (v. 23).
claims.evidence: Ruth 2 read in full, Hebrew with JPS English (Mechon Mamre); 23 verses verified by live count. Keil & Delitzsch's chapter summary divides the chapter the same way (vv. 1–16; vv. 17–23).

claims.claim: Boaz is introduced as a kinsman of Elimelech, a *gibbor chayil*; here the phrase means a man of property and standing, not a warrior.
claims.evidence: Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:1 ("here it signifies a man of property"); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ("a mighty man of wealth"). Both agree against the military sense (cf. Judg 6:12; 11:1).

claims.claim: The field's corners are not to be wholly reaped, the fallen grain is not to be gathered, the vineyard is not to be gone over a second time, and fallen grapes are not to be picked up; all are left for the poor and the stranger.
claims.evidence: Lev 19:9–10 read in full in Hebrew with JPS English (Mechon Mamre, `pt0319.htm`, 37 verses verified live): "thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleaning of thy harvest" (v. 9); "thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger" (v. 10). Corroborated by BiblicalTraining, "Gleaning."

claims.claim: Four distinct provisions: (1) field-corner and fallen-grain gleaning (Lev 19:9); (2) the forgotten sheaf (Deut 24:19); (3) olive-beating, the tree not gone over twice (Deut 24:20); (4) vineyard second-gleaning (Lev 19:10; Deut 24:21). They differ in object, act and verb (*laqat* "pick up" vs *'alal* "go over a second time").
claims.evidence: Lev 19:9–10 and Deut 24:19–22 read in full (Mechon Mamre; Deut 24:19 JPS: "When thou reapest thy harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go back to fetch it"). BiblicalTraining, "Gleaning" (terms section: *laqat*/*leqet*, *'alal*/*'olelot*, *pe'ah*, *peret*). Reuse: `clm-deu-06-063` (established) states the Deut 24 trio.

claims.claim: Gleaning behind the reapers among the sheaves was a privilege of the owner's goodwill, beyond the law's bare requirement; Ruth seeks a field where she will find favour, and asks the overseer's leave.
claims.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:2: the right of gleaning was conferred by positive law, "but liberty to glean behind the reapers was not a right that could be claimed; it was a privilege granted or refused according to the good will or favor of the owner." Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:2–3: the law secured the right, but hard-hearted farmers obstructed the poor.

claims.claim: Boaz's protection: Ruth is to glean only in his field, stay close by his maidens, and drink from the vessels the young men have drawn; he has charged the young men not to touch her (to do her no harm).
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:8–9 read in full. Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:8: the maidens tie the sheaves while the men cut; "I have commanded the young men not to touch thee (to do thee no harm)." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:8–9: Boaz "provided for her personal comfort"; the vessels were skin bottles of water.

claims.claim: Boaz orders his young men to let Ruth glean even among the sheaves without shaming her, and to pull stalks deliberately from the bundles and leave them for her — orders that go far beyond the bounds of generosity and compassion for the poor.
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:15–16 read in full. Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:15: "These directions of Boaz went far beyond the bounds of generosity and compassion for the poor." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:16: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her."

claims.claim: At mealtime Boaz invites Ruth to eat bread dipped in vinegar beside the reapers and has parched corn served to her; she eats, is satisfied, and has some left over, which she carries home to Naomi.
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:14, 18 read in full. Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:14: *chometz*, a sour beverage of vinegar mixed with oil; *qali*, roasted grains of wheat, still eaten by reapers on the harvest field. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:14: the bread soaked in vinegar, "a kind of poor, weak wine"; the parched corn "roasted on the spot, and fit for use after being rubbed in the hands."

claims.claim: The ephah is the standard dry measure: ten omers (Exod 16:36), one-tenth of a homer, equal in capacity to the liquid bath (Ezek 45:11). Ruth threshed "about an ephah of barley" from one day's gleaning.
claims.evidence: Brown-Driver-Briggs H374 (read in full): "a certain quantity of wheat, barley, etc. = ten omers (Exodus 16:36) … = 1/10 chomer (Ezekiel 45:11) (= bath)," listing Ruth 2:17 among the occurrences. Ruth 2:17 read in full.

claims.claim: In modern terms an ephah is about 20–22 litres (roughly 25–30 lbs of barley); a yield of that size from one day's gleaning is unusually large and signals Boaz's generosity.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Ephah (measure)" (read in full): most modern estimates 13–23 litres, about 20 litres / half a bushel most commonly; jar fragments at Lachish and Tell Beit Mirsim suggest about 22 litres (second-hand here — excavation reports not read). Keil & Delitzsch: "about 20–25 lbs." BiblicalTraining, "Gleaning": "probably about 30 pounds (13 kg)." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown's "about a bushel" is now generally regarded as too large (BiblicalTraining, "Ephah"). The range, not a single figure, is what the evidence supports.

claims.claim: Barley ripens first (about April) and wheat follows weeks later (about May–June); Ruth gleaned from the start of barley harvest to the end of wheat harvest — about seven weeks, the count from putting the sickle to the standing grain to the Feast of Weeks.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Harvest" and "Reaping" (read in full): barley cut in about April, wheat reaped in about May and June, the grain harvest lasting about seven weeks (Deut 16:9). ISBE, "Harvest" (Patch): Passover in April at the barley harvest, Pentecost seven weeks later at the wheat harvest; "between the reaping of the barley in April and the wheat in June, most of the other cereals are reaped." Months are modern approximations varying with elevation.

claims.claim: "Under whose wings thou art come to take refuge" (2:12): *kanaph* is wing / edge / extremity; Brown-Driver-Briggs lists Ruth 2:12 under YHWH as protector (cf. Ps 91:4; 36:8; 57:2) and Ruth 3:9 under the garment sense of the same word.
claims.evidence: Brown-Driver-Briggs H3671 (read in full): §1h, figurative of YHWH as protector, citing Ps 17:8; 36:8; 57:2; 61:5; 63:3; 91:4; Ruth 2:12; §2a, of garment = skirt, corner, citing Ruth 3:9 (*k'napekha*). Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:11: the figure is derived from Deut 32:11; cf. Ps 91:4; 36:8; 57:2.

claims.claim: The wording of 2:12 is the image the threshing-floor scene answers — a deliberate anticipation of 3:9.
claims.evidence: Brown-Driver-Briggs H3671 (read in full) lists Ruth 2:12 under YHWH as protector and Ruth 3:9 under the garment sense of the same word. The anticipation of 3:9 is a literary reading: the shared word is established; the deliberate foreshadowing is probable, not stated by the text.

claims.claim: Naomi names Boaz "one of our redeemers" (*miggo'aleinu*): the *go'el* is first named here, and the redeemer thread is carried from this verse into chapters 3–4.
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:20 read in full. Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:19–20: "one of our redeemers"; on the *go'el*, see Lev 25:26, 48–49.

claims.claim: The governing classification — redemption by a *go'el*, not levirate marriage under Deut 25:5–10 — is reused from the published record.
claims.evidence: Reuse: `clm-deu-06-069` (probable), `clm-deu-06-076` (probable), `conn-deu-06-058` (probable). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown's looser gloss ("to protect us, to purchase our lands, and marry you") is noted in §8 as superseded for Gnosis purposes.

claims.claim: Ruth is designated "the Moabitess" three times in this chapter (2:2, 6, 21), and her foreignness is stressed. This stands in tension with the Deut 23:3 exclusion of the Moabite from the assembly; the tension is noted, not resolved.
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:2, 6, 21 read in full. Reuse: `clm-deu-06-043` (established, the exclusion); `clm-deu-06-045` (established, its text-internal rationale: inhospitality and the hiring of Balaam); `conn-deu-06-023` (probable: "the tension with the exclusion is noted, not resolved"). Per Yonatan's decision (2026-11-23), this dossier documents the tension without imposing a resolution; no source read for R02 establishes any resolution (see §8). Resolution: unknown.

claims.claim: The harvest workforce is headed by a servant set over the reapers, who superintends the work, supplies provisions and pays the labourers in the evening; work runs from morning until evening, with brief rest in a field shelter.
claims.evidence: Ruth 2:5–7, 17 read in full. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:5 (the overseer's duties) and 2:7 (field labours begun early in the morning; "the house" as the field tent for rest and refreshment). Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:4–7 (the overseer's threefold report). The "field tent" reading of 2:7 is probable at most (see §8).

claims.claim: The gender division of the harvest labour (who cuts, who binds/sheaves) is disputed between the commentaries.
claims.evidence: Keil & Delitzsch on Ruth 2:8: the maidens tie up the sheaves whilst the men-servants cut the corn. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ruth 2:8: "The reaping was performed by women while the assortment of sheaves was the duty of men-servants." The two accounts cannot both be right as stated; the dossier records the disagreement.

claims.claim: The Gezer Calendar lists a month of barley harvest followed by a month of general harvest; it is conventionally dated to the 10th century BCE by its script, was found unstratified in 1908, and its script, language and purpose are debated.
claims.evidence: Dospěl, "The Gezer Calendar," *Bible History Daily* (Biblical Archaeology Society), 12 Aug 2026 (read in full): "Thought to date from the tenth century BCE"; "does not come from a secure archaeological context"; script Phoenician or Old Hebrew, language Hebrew, Canaanite or Phoenician; purpose almanac, writing exercise or blessing tablet.

claims.claim: No archaeological evidence ties any site to Boaz's field or verifies the events of Ruth 2; threshing floors and gates are attested only in general Iron Age terms.
claims.evidence: No site, excavation, inscription or artifact for Ruth 2 was found in the sources read for this dossier or in the existing library (see §2, §6). Reuse: Deuteronomy 06 dossier line 151 (general material attestation only). Absence of evidence is recorded as unknown, not as disproof.

connections.note: Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, from her arrival in the field to the end of the barley and wheat harvests.
Naomi and Ruth reach Bethlehem as the barley harvest begins, setting the season in which the gleaning takes place.
The field's corners are left unreaped and fallen grain ungathered, and the vineyard is not gone over twice; the remainder is left for the poor and the stranger.
The same gleaning rule is set beside the Feast of Weeks, tying the joy of the wheat harvest to care for people who own no land.
A forgotten sheaf, olives left after beating, and grapes left after gathering belong to the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

The law excludes Moabites from the assembly, while Ruth the Moabitess is welcomed into the field, protected, and blessed; the tension is recorded here without resolving it. (English verse numbering; the Hebrew text numbers this verse 23:4.)
The LORD is pictured as an eagle spreading its wings over its young, the image behind Boaz's blessing about refuge under God's wings.
Shelter under his wings: the psalm's refuge image is the same picture Boaz uses for Ruth.
Ruth asks Boaz to spread his wing, the corner of his garment, over her — the same Hebrew word as the wings of refuge in chapter 2.
A near kinsman may redeem land sold in poverty; the kin-redemption framework behind the redeemer named in chapter 2.
A near kinsman may redeem a person who has sold himself; the same redeemer word covers land and people.
Gideon prepares unleavened bread from an ephah of flour; the same household measure Ruth carries home.
Jesse sends David to his brothers with an ephah of parched grain; the same measure, and the same food Ruth ate at the meal.
Seven weeks are counted from putting the sickle to the standing grain to the Feast of Weeks; the harvest calendar Ruth's season follows.
An omer is a tenth of an ephah; the ratio that fixes the measure Ruth's yield is given in.
The ephah and the bath are the same size, each a tenth of a homer.
Gideon answers Ephraim with a proverb about the gleaning of Ephraim's grapes; gleaning was a familiar picture for what is left after the main gathering.
Leaving father, mother and homeland at God's call, as Boaz says Ruth has done in coming to a people she did not know.
At the gate Boaz declares he has acquired the field and taken Ruth as wife; the redemption named in chapter 2 is carried out there.
